name: Delaware
note: In Delaware the funeral director who takes custody of the body files the death certificate with the Office of Vital Statistics (Division of Public Health) within three days of death and before final disposition. Filing is entirely electronic, through the Delaware Vital Events Registration System (DelVERS). The attending physician, APRN or physician associate certifies within 48 hours. Deaths needing an official investigation go to the Medical Examiner (Division of Forensic Science), who also signs every cremation permit. From registration, state law sends a monthly death file to the Department of Elections and the State Election Commissioner, who must cancel those voters, and releases data to the state's Health Statistics Center and national statistics. Certified copies are restricted to the registrant's spouse, children, parents or guardian and people who need the record to protect a personal or property right.

steps.title: Pronounce death
steps.who: The attending physician; the medical examiner; a registered nurse or APRN; the medical control physician (emergency medical services); or a physician associate.
steps.summary: Delaware's registration statute itself lists who may pronounce a death, and registered nurses are included.

steps.title: Report reportable deaths to the Medical Examiner
steps.who: Any person having knowledge of the death. The Medical Examiner then notifies the Attorney General.
steps.trigger: Violence, suicide, casualty, anaesthesia, poison or overdose, sudden death in apparent health, an unattended death, death in prison or police custody, occupational disease, a public-health threat, a suspicious or unusual death, or an unclaimed body.
steps.summary: Wilfully failing to report is punishable by up to a year in prison or a $1,000 fine. When an official death investigation is required, the Medical Examiner takes custody, determines cause and manner, and completes and files the death certificate.

steps.title: Certify the cause of death electronically
steps.who: The attending physician, an APRN or a physician associate; failing them, a designated physician or the institution's chief medical officer who knows the history.
steps.trigger: A death not requiring an official investigation; the funeral director sends the personal data for certification.
steps.summary: The medical certification must be prepared, certified and signed electronically. If the cause cannot be determined within 48 hours, a pending certificate is filed and a toxicology study is done, and unresolved cases go to the Division of Forensic Science.

steps.title: File the death certificate in DelVERS
steps.who: The funeral director who assumes custody of the body, who gets the personal data from the next of kin or the best qualified source.

deadline.text: within 3 days after death and prior to final disposition

steps.summary: The certificate is filed electronically with the Office of Vital Statistics through DelVERS, and is registered once complete. Wilfully neglecting a duty under the chapter is punishable by up to one year in prison or a $1,000 fine.

steps.title: Burial or transit permit must accompany the body
steps.who: The funeral director, who hands the permit to the cemetery sexton or keeps it with cremated remains.
steps.summary: A body may not be disposed of until the burial or transit permit is completed. Moving a body without a permit is an offence. The text read here does not say who issues the permit.

steps.title: Medical Examiner signs every cremation permit
steps.who: The chief, assistant or deputy medical examiner. The permit is presented with the physician-signed death certificate and the next of kin's authorisation.
steps.trigger: Intended cremation or natural organic reduction, including when the body is removed to another state for it.
steps.summary: Signing affirms there is no medical reason against cremation, and the ME may hold the remains for investigation. A copy of the permit goes with the death certificate to the Office of Vital Statistics.

steps.title: Certified copies to close family or those protecting a right
steps.who: The registrant's spouse, children, parents or guardian, or their authorised representatives. Others who show the record is needed to determine or protect a personal or property right, or for genealogy.
steps.summary: Vital records are confidential except as the chapter and regulations allow. Death records become public 40 years after the death. Appeals from a custodian's refusal go to the Department.

steps.title: State Health Statistics Center and national vital statistics
steps.who: The Delaware Health Statistics Center (Division of Public Health); by agreement, the federal agency responsible for national vital statistics and other states' vital records offices.
steps.summary: The Health Statistics Center analyses and publishes vital statistics. The State Registrar may send copies of records to the national statistics agency, and to other states for their residents, for statistical or administrative use.

steps.title: Monthly death file to the Department of Elections
steps.who: The Office of Vital Statistics, to the Department of Elections and the State Election Commissioner.
steps.trigger: Deaths of persons 16 or older reported in the State since the last report. A twice-yearly file (January and July) covers Delaware residents who died in another state or country.
steps.summary: The file gives name, social security number, residence, dates of birth and death, and certificate number. The Department of Elections must cancel each listed voter.

steps.title: Family or obituary notice to cancel a voter registration
steps.who: The decedent's spouse, adult child, sibling or parent (written notice or death certificate copy), or a Delaware newspaper obituary for deaths out of state.
steps.summary: The Department may also cancel a registration on these sources.

steps.title: Private bodies rely on certified copies
steps.who: The family or personal representative, who presents a certified copy. Non-family institutions may apply themselves only by showing a personal or property right.
steps.summary: No Delaware statute read here gives banks or insurers a data route to vital records. Private-sector verification runs through the federal layer (LADMF).

steps.title: Register of Wills advertises the grant of letters
steps.who: The Register of Wills of the county where the decedent lived.
steps.trigger: Grant of letters testamentary or of administration.

deadline.text: posted within 40 days from the grant of letters

steps.summary: The notice gives the date of death and the personal representative. It is posted on the county website or at the courthouse, and published in a newspaper weekly for three weeks, except for small estates (personal estate of $30,000 or less and total estate of $35,000 or less).

registrationDeadlineDays.note: Within 3 days after death and before final disposition.

informantDuty.note: The funeral director who takes custody files the certificate; the Medical Examiner files in investigated cases. Next of kin only supply personal data.

medicalExaminerScrutiny.note: No review of every certificate, but the Medical Examiner must be notified of, and must sign the permit for, every cremation or natural organic reduction.

electronicRegistration.note: Medical certifications must be prepared and signed electronically, and all death certificates filed in DelVERS.

centralPopulationRegister.note: No population register; the Office of Vital Statistics under the State Registrar holds the record.

governmentPropagation.note: Under state law, a registered death reaches the Department of Elections automatically (a monthly file, with mandatory cancellation) and goes to state and national statistics. No state provision found reaches the DMV, Medicaid or the Division of Revenue. Federal feeds (SSA) are in the us-federal layer.

certificateAccess.note: Spouse, children, parents, guardian or their representatives; others who show a personal or property right, or for genealogy. Public after 40 years.

gaps: Pointer 15 Del. C. § 1703 concerns felony convictions. The death provision is § 1705, cited instead.

16 Del. C. §§ 3101, 3105, 3121, 3123 and 3127 each have two versions on delcode (one 'effective until' and one effective Dec. 6, 2026 or on a contingency in 85 Del. Laws, c. 459). Both versions of § 3123 were read and are the same on every point used here. Only a cross-reference to Title 24 changes.

The Delaware Administrative Code (regulations.delaware.gov) is a script-rendered app and was not read. The Division of Public Health vital statistics regulations, which define who else may obtain copies and may set a burial-permit procedure, are not cited.
Who issues the burial-transit permit under § 3151 was not established from the text read (subchapter III does not say).
No state statute was found sending deaths to the Division of Motor Vehicles, Delaware Medicaid or the Division of Revenue. Titles 21, 30 and 31 were not searched.
No Delaware provision read here mentions an electronic death feed to SSA. It is left to the us-federal layer.
privateSectorVerification is left to the us-federal layer (LADMF). Delaware law gives private bodies no vital records route beyond applying for a copy on a property-right basis.
